chunks.summary: A decoder is a combinational circuit that activates exactly one of M outputs for each unique combination of N input bits, identifying a specific binary code.
chunks.text: A decoder accepts a set of inputs that represents a binary number and activates only the output that corresponds to that input number. Decoder inputs often come from the outputs of a counter or register. For each input combination, only one of the M outputs is active (HIGH), while all other outputs remain LOW; this is called an active-HIGH decoder because the selected output goes HIGH. Many decoders are instead designed to produce active-LOW outputs, where only the selected output goes LOW while all others stay HIGH. A decoder is said to identify, recognize, or detect a particular input code.
chunks.figure_note: Page 6 shows a block diagram of a decoder with N inputs representing a binary number and M outputs, where for each input combination only one of the M outputs is HIGH (active-HIGH) or LOW (active-LOW) while the rest sit at the opposite level.

chunks.summary: A 3-input, 8-output AND-gate decoder circuit where each AND gate decodes one unique combination of the true/complemented inputs A, B, C to drive its corresponding active-HIGH output.
chunks.text: A decoder with three inputs (A, B, C) and eight outputs (O0-O7) can be built entirely from AND gates: each input is buffered to produce both its true and complemented form, and each of the 8 AND gates takes the unique combination of true/complemented A, B, C needed to recognize one input code. Because the circuit uses AND gates, its outputs are active-HIGH -- e.g., output O6 goes HIGH only when CBA = 110(2) = 6(10). This circuit is called a 3-line-to-8-line decoder (three input lines, eight output lines), also known as a binary-to-octal decoder/converter (it takes a 3-bit binary code and activates one of eight octal outputs), and also a 1-of-8 decoder because only one of the eight outputs is ever activated at a time.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 7-8 show the full AND-gate schematic: three inputs A2/A1/A0(MSB) each buffered into true/complement lines feeding into 8 AND gates whose outputs O7..O0 are each active-HIGH for one unique input code.

chunks.summary: Enable inputs let a decoder be turned on or off: when enabled the A,B,C inputs select the active output as normal, but when disabled all outputs are forced to their inactive level regardless of A,B,C.
chunks.text: Some decoders have one or more ENABLE inputs used to control the decoder's operation. With a common ENABLE line connected to an extra input of every output gate: if ENABLE is HIGH, the decoder functions normally and the A, B, C inputs determine which output is HIGH; if ENABLE is LOW, all outputs are forced LOW regardless of the levels at A, B, C. This allows a decoder to be selectively activated, which is essential when combining/cascading decoders or gating them from a larger system.

chunks.summary: The 74ALS138 is a commercial 3-to-8 line decoder with three active-LOW enable inputs (E1-bar, E2-bar) and one active-HIGH enable (E3), producing eight active-LOW outputs based on address inputs A2A1A0.
chunks.text: The 74ALS138 is a widely used 1-of-8 decoder IC. It has three address inputs A2, A1, A0 (A2 is the MSB) and eight active-LOW outputs O7-bar through O0-bar (only the selected output goes LOW; all others stay HIGH). It provides three ENABLE inputs: two active-LOW (E1-bar, E2-bar) and one active-HIGH (E3). The decoder responds to the input code A2A1A0 only when E1-bar=0 AND E2-bar=0 AND E3=1; any other combination of the enable inputs disables the decoder and forces all outputs HIGH. This enable logic makes it easy to cascade multiple 74ALS138 chips to build larger decoders, or to use one as an address-range decoder/demultiplexer in a larger system.
chunks.figure_note: Page 10 (image page) shows: the internal AND-gate logic diagram of the 74ALS138 (three buffered address inputs A2A1A0 feeding 8 AND gates, gated by a 3-input AND combining E1-bar, E2-bar, E3), the IC block symbol with data[2..0]/enable inputs and eq0-eq7 outputs, the external pinout diagram (A2 A1 A0 in, O7-bar..O0-bar out, E1-bar E2-bar E3 enable group), and the enable truth table: E1-bar E2-bar E3 = 0,0,1 -> respond to input code A2A1A0; any of 1,X,X / X,1,X / X,X,0 -> disabled, all outputs HIGH.

chunks.summary: The 7442 is a BCD-to-decimal decoder with no enable input; the 7445 is a similar BCD-to-decimal decoder/driver with open-collector outputs suited to directly driving higher-current loads like LEDs, lamps, relays, or dc motors.
chunks.text: The 7442 is a BCD-to-decimal decoder: it takes a 4-bit BCD code and activates one of ten decimal outputs; unlike the 74ALS138 it does not have an enable input. The 7445 is also a BCD-to-decimal decoder, but is called a 'driver' because it has open-collector outputs that can operate at higher current and voltage limits than a normal TTL output, making it suitable for directly driving loads such as indicator LEDs, lamps, relays, or dc motors -- loads a standard TTL output could not safely drive.

chunks.summary: A 7-segment display shows decimal/hex digits using seven individually controllable segments, commonly implemented with LEDs; a BCD-to-7-segment decoder/driver turns on the correct combination of segments for a given BCD input code.
chunks.text: The 7-segment display is a common way to display decimal or hexadecimal characters. One common arrangement uses a light-emitting diode (LED) for each of the seven segments. A diode allows current to flow in only one direction; when the LED's anode is more positive than its cathode by about 2 V, the LED lights up. By controlling the current through each of the seven LED segments, some segments are turned on (emitting light) while others stay off, producing the desired character pattern. A BCD-to-7-segment decoder/driver IC activates the specific pattern of segments needed to display the decimal digit corresponding to its BCD input code.

chunks.topic: The 7446/47 BCD-to-7-Segment Decoder/Driver and Common-Anode vs Common-Cathode Displays
chunks.summary: The 7446/47 activates the correct segment pattern for each BCD input code; common-anode displays tie all segment anodes to Vcc (segments driven active-LOW), while common-cathode displays tie all cathodes together and typically need a transistor interface since TTL/CMOS outputs cannot drive them directly.
chunks.text: The 7446/7447 is a BCD-to-7-segment decoder/driver that activates the specific segment pattern corresponding to each BCD input code. In a common-anode LED display, the anodes of all seven segments are tied together to Vcc, so each segment is turned on by pulling its cathode LOW (active-LOW segment drive) -- this is the type used by the 7446/47. A different arrangement, the common-cathode display, ties all segment cathodes together instead; each segment there typically needs 10 to 20 mA of drive current, and standard TTL/CMOS devices are normally not used to drive a common-cathode display directly -- a transistor interface circuit is often required to supply that current.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 15-16 (image pages) show block/pin diagrams of the 7446/47 BCD-to-7-segment decoder/driver and a common-anode 7-segment LED display schematic where all segment anodes tie to Vcc and each segment cathode is pulled low through the driver to light that segment.

chunks.summary: An LCD does not emit its own light but controls the reflection or transmission of available light through a segment; applying voltage across a segment turns it on (blocks/scatters light) while zero voltage leaves it off, and LCDs consume far less power than LEDs though LEDs are brighter in the dark.
chunks.text: A liquid-crystal display (LCD) works by controlling the reflection of available light rather than emitting light itself. The available light may be ambient light (room or sunlight) -- these are reflective LCDs -- or it may come from a small light source built into the display unit, called a backlit LCD. LCDs have gained wide acceptance because of their very low power consumption compared to LEDs. LEDs, on the other hand, have the advantage of a much brighter display that remains easily visible in dark or poorly lit areas. In the basic segment arrangement, zero voltage across a segment leaves it OFF (transparent/reflective), while applying an ac voltage between the segment electrode and a common backplane electrode turns that segment ON (it becomes visibly dark against the background).
chunks.figure_note: Page 18 shows the basic LCD segment arrangement: a segment electrode and a backplane electrode sandwiching the liquid-crystal material; zero voltage across them leaves the segment OFF, applying voltage between segment and backplane turns the segment ON.

chunks.topic: Driving an LCD 7-Segment Display with AC
chunks.summary: LCD segments must be driven with an ac waveform rather than dc; this is commonly done by applying out-of-phase square waves to the segment electrode and the backplane so a net effective voltage exists across the segment only when it is meant to be on.
chunks.text: LCD segments require an alternating (ac) drive voltage rather than a steady dc voltage, because a sustained dc voltage across the liquid crystal degrades it over time. A common way to produce the required ac voltage is to apply out-of-phase square waves to the segment electrode and to the backplane electrode: when the two waveforms are out of phase, there is a net ac voltage difference across the segment (turning it ON); when segment and backplane are driven in phase, the net voltage across the segment averages to zero (segment OFF).
chunks.figure_note: Page 19 (image page) shows waveform timing diagrams of the segment drive signal and backplane drive signal (out-of-phase square waves) for a 7-segment LCD, illustrating how phase relationship determines whether a segment is ON or OFF.

chunks.topic: Multidigit, Alphanumeric, and Graphical/Color LCD Modules
chunks.summary: Beyond simple numeric 7-segment displays, LCDs are available as multidigit numeric displays, alphanumeric character modules (up to 4 lines x 40 characters), and graphical dot-matrix panels controlled by row/column scanning, with color panels using three subpixels (red/green/blue) per pixel.
chunks.text: Liquid crystals are available as multidigit 7-segment decimal numeric displays. Alphanumeric LCD modules are available in many formats, up to 4 lines by 40 characters. Other LCD modules let the user create a graphical display by controlling individual dots on the screen, called pixels. Larger LCD panels can be scanned at a high rate to produce high-quality video motion pictures; their control lines are arranged in rows and columns, and a digital system must activate a matrix row/column intersection to control the amount of light at each pixel. On a color display, each pixel is made up of three subpixels that control light passing through a red, green, or blue filter to produce the pixel's color -- for example, a 640 x 480 color LCD screen would need 640 x 3 column connections plus 480 row connections, a total of 2400 connections to the LCD. Older screens are called Twisted Nematic (TN) or Super Twisted Nematic (STN) and are referred to as passive LCDs; newer displays are active-matrix TFT LCDs, which use an active switching element at each pixel. Other display technologies include vacuum fluorescent, gas discharge plasma, and electroluminescent displays -- the optical physics differs for each, but the means of controlling all of them (activating rows/columns or segments with digital signals) is fundamentally the same.

chunks.summary: An encoder performs the opposite function of a decoder: it has M input lines (normally only one active at a time) and produces an N-bit binary output code identifying which input line was activated.
chunks.text: Most decoders accept an input code and produce an active output at one and only one output line -- a decoder identifies, recognizes, or detects a particular code. The opposite operation is encoding, performed by a logic circuit called an encoder. An encoder has a number of input lines (M), only one of which is activated at a given time; the inputs are typically active-HIGH, meaning they are normally LOW and become HIGH when activated. The encoder produces an N-bit output code depending on which single input line is activated.
chunks.figure_note: Page 24 shows a block diagram of a generic encoder with M active-HIGH input lines (normally LOW, only one active at a time) and N output lines producing the corresponding binary code.

chunks.summary: An octal-to-binary encoder accepts eight input lines and produces a three-bit binary output code corresponding to whichever single input is active; it only works correctly when exactly one input is active at a time.
chunks.text: An octal-to-binary encoder, also called an 8-line-to-3-line encoder, accepts eight input lines and produces a three-bit output code corresponding to whichever input line is active. A basic logic circuit for this can be built from OR gates, where each of the three output bits is the OR of the input lines whose binary index has that bit set. This basic (non-priority) encoder design requires that only one input be active at any one time; if two or more inputs are active simultaneously, the OR-gate combination produces an output code that does not correctly correspond to any single input.
chunks.figure_note: Page 25 shows the OR-gate logic circuit for an octal-to-binary (8-line-to-3-line) encoder: eight input lines D0-D7 combined through OR gates to produce a 3-bit output code A2A1A0.

chunks.summary: A priority encoder resolves the ambiguity of multiple simultaneously active inputs by always outputting the code for the highest-numbered active input, e.g. a 9-input BCD priority encoder with active-LOW inputs for digits 1-9.
chunks.text: A priority encoder ensures that when two or more inputs are activated at the same time, the output code corresponds to the highest-numbered active input, resolving the ambiguity that a simple (non-priority) encoder cannot handle. An example priority encoder has nine active-LOW inputs representing decimal digits 1 through 9; it produces an inverted BCD code corresponding to whichever is the highest-numbered activated input, ignoring any lower-numbered inputs that happen to be active simultaneously.

chunks.summary: A switch encoder converts manual keypad/switch entry into BCD; the 74LS147 is a priority encoder used for this purpose so that if multiple keys are pressed simultaneously, the BCD code for the highest-numbered key is produced.
chunks.text: A switch encoder can be used whenever BCD data must be entered manually into a digital system -- for example, the 10 switches might be the keyboard switches on a calculator, representing digits 0 through 9. The switches are normally-open, so the encoder inputs are all normally HIGH and the BCD output defaults to 0000 with no key pressed. When a key is pressed, the circuit produces the BCD code for that digit. The 74LS147 is a priority encoder, so if more than one key is pressed simultaneously, it produces the BCD code for the higher-numbered key, avoiding an invalid or ambiguous output.

chunks.topic: Troubleshooting MSI Circuits: Observation, Analysis, Divide-and-Conquer
chunks.summary: As circuit complexity grows, systematic observation and analysis, combined with a repeated divide-and-conquer strategy, are used to narrow down the possible location of a fault.
chunks.text: More complex circuitry increases the number of possible reasons for a failure. Applying careful observation and analysis narrows the focus and simplifies testing. The recommended troubleshooting method is: first use observation and analysis to determine the set of possible faults, then repeatedly apply the divide-and-conquer technique -- testing a point roughly midway through the suspect circuitry to determine which half contains the fault -- to cut the remaining possible causes in half at each step, converging quickly on the actual faulty component or connection.

chunks.summary: A multiplexer (MUX), or data selector, is a combinational circuit that selects one of N input data sources and routes it to a single output line, with the choice controlled by SELECT (address) inputs.
chunks.text: A multiplexer (MUX) selects one of N input data sources and transmits the selected data to a single output line; this operation is called multiplexing. A digital multiplexer, also called a data selector, is a logic circuit that performs this task. Routing of the desired data input to the output is controlled by SELECT inputs, which are also referred to as ADDRESS inputs because the binary value on the select lines addresses which data input is passed through. Two-, four-, eight-, and 16-input multiplexers are available as standard ICs in both TTL and CMOS logic families, and these basic ICs can be combined (cascaded) to multiplex a larger number of inputs than a single chip supports.
chunks.figure_note: Page 30 shows a block diagram of a multiplexer: N data inputs, a set of SELECT/ADDRESS input lines, and a single output; the select code determines which one of the N inputs is routed to the output.

chunks.summary: The 74ALS157 IC packages four independent two-input multiplexers on a single chip, sharing common select and enable lines.
chunks.text: The 74ALS157 contains four separate two-input multiplexers in one package. Because the four multiplexer sections typically share a common SELECT input and a common enable/strobe input, the chip can, for example, select one of two 4-bit data words and route it to a 4-bit output bus with a single select line -- a common use case being switching between two different clock sources or two different data buses.

chunks.summary: Multiplexers are used throughout digital systems for data selection/routing, parallel-to-serial conversion, operation sequencing, and generating arbitrary waveforms or logic functions from a truth table.
chunks.text: Multiplexer circuits find numerous and varied applications in digital systems of all types, including: data selection and routing (choosing among several data sources); parallel-to-serial conversion (successively selecting each bit of a parallel word to build a serial bit stream); operation sequencing (stepping through a sequence of operations); and waveform or logic-function generation (using a multiplexer's data inputs, tied HIGH/LOW according to a truth table, and its select lines as the function's variables, so the multiplexer output directly implements the desired logic function).

chunks.topic: Example: Multiplexing Two BCD Counter Displays
chunks.summary: A system that uses a multiplexer to route two separate multidigit BCD counters to a shared display, showing one counter at a time (e.g. under operator control or on a timed switch).
chunks.text: One application example shows a system for displaying two multidigit BCD counters on a single shared display, one counter at a time. A multiplexer selects which counter's BCD outputs are routed to the display-driving circuitry based on a select signal, so only one counter's value is visible at any moment even though both counters keep counting independently in the background.
chunks.figure_note: Page 35 shows a block diagram: two multidigit BCD counters feeding into a multiplexer, whose select input picks one counter's outputs at a time to drive the shared decoder/display.

chunks.topic: Example: Parallel-to-Serial Conversion with a Multiplexer
chunks.summary: A multiplexer can convert an 8-bit parallel word into a serial bit stream by cycling its select (address) inputs through 0-7 so each data bit X7..X0 is placed on the output one at a time in sequence.
chunks.text: A multiplexer used as a parallel-to-serial converter takes an 8-bit parallel word (X7 X6 X5 X4 X3 X2 X1 X0) applied to its eight data inputs, and a counter or sequencer drives the select inputs through the binary values 0 through 7 in turn. As the select code steps through each value, the multiplexer output presents each data bit in turn, producing a serial bit stream. For the example parallel word 10110101, stepping the select inputs generates that same bit pattern serially on the multiplexer's single output line over eight successive select states.
chunks.figure_note: Page 36 shows the parallel-to-serial converter block diagram (8-bit parallel input X7-X0 into an 8-input MUX, select inputs driven by a 3-bit counter) plus the resulting output waveform for input pattern 10110101 as the select code counts from 0 to 7.

chunks.topic: Example: Implementing a Logic Function with a Multiplexer
chunks.summary: Any truth table can be implemented directly with a multiplexer by connecting the truth table's input variables to the MUX select lines and hard-wiring each data input to the truth table's corresponding output value (0 or 1).
chunks.text: A multiplexer can implement an arbitrary combinational logic function described by a truth table without any additional gates: the function's input variables are connected to the multiplexer's select (address) inputs, and each multiplexer data input is tied HIGH or LOW according to the truth table's output value for that combination of select-line values. Since the select lines choose exactly the data input corresponding to the current combination of input variables, the multiplexer output directly reproduces the truth table's output column.
chunks.figure_note: Page 37 (image page) shows a multiplexer whose select inputs are wired to the function's input variables and whose data inputs are each tied HIGH or LOW per the accompanying truth table, so the MUX output reproduces the specified logic function.

chunks.summary: A demultiplexer (DEMUX) is the inverse of a multiplexer: it takes a single data input and distributes it to one of several outputs, with the select code determining which output receives the data.
chunks.text: A demultiplexer (DEMUX) takes a single input and distributes it over several outputs; the select input code determines to which output the DATA input will be transmitted. A 1-line-to-8-line demultiplexer, for example, has one data input, three select lines (S2 S1 S0), and eight outputs O0-O7; the select code chooses exactly one output to receive (and reproduce) the data input, while all other outputs are held at their inactive level. Its truth table shows, for each of the eight select codes, which single output carries the data input value 'I' while the rest read 0.
chunks.figure_note: Page 39 (image page) shows a 1-line-to-8-line demultiplexer built from inverters (generating complemented S2,S1,S0) and eight 4-input AND gates, each producing one output Ox = I . (unique combination of S2,S1,S0), plus the full select-code/output truth table confirming only the selected output equals the data input I for each of the 8 select codes 000-111.

chunks.topic: Example: Security Monitoring System Using a Demultiplexer/Decoder (74ALS138)
chunks.summary: A 74ALS138 used as an 8-output demultiplexer can scan and report the status of eight door switches in a security system, where each door switch output is HIGH when its door is open and LOW when closed.
chunks.text: A security monitoring system can use the 74ALS138 (functioning here as a demultiplexer/decoder) to handle up to eight doors, expandable to any number by adding more decoder chips. Door switches serve as data inputs to the system: each door switch produces a HIGH when its door is open and a LOW when it is closed. By scanning the select/address inputs of the 74ALS138, the system can sequentially check each door's status through the corresponding output line.

chunks.topic: Example: Synchronous Serial Data Transmission System (MUX + DEMUX)
chunks.summary: A synchronous transmission system pairs a multiplexer at the transmitter (parallel-to-serial, serializing four 4-bit words) with a demultiplexer at the receiver (serial-to-parallel, distributing bits back into four separate storage registers), synchronized by a shared timing scheme.
chunks.text: A synchronous data transmission system can be used to transmit four separate 4-bit words serially from a transmitter to a remote receiver. At the transmitter, a multiplexer loads the four 4-bit parallel words and serializes them bit by bit onto a single transmission line, synchronized to a clock. At the receiver, the corresponding block distributes (demultiplexes) the incoming serial bit stream back into the four separate 4-bit registers, storing each word as it arrives. A timing diagram illustrates the parallel data loaded into the transmitter, the resulting serial bit stream on the transmission line, and how that stream is distributed to and stored in the four receiver registers over time.

chunks.topic: More Troubleshooting: Applying Observation and Analysis to an MSI Circuit
chunks.summary: A worked troubleshooting example asks the student to apply observation and analysis to a test result on an MSI circuit and determine the most probable fault.
chunks.text: This section presents a worked example applying the observation-and-analysis troubleshooting approach introduced earlier (Section 9-5) to a specific MSI circuit. Given a test performed on the circuit and the resulting (unexpected) output, the exercise is to reason about which single fault -- such as a stuck input/output, an open connection, or a miswired enable -- would produce exactly that observed result, using the same systematic narrowing process.
chunks.figure_note: Page 44 shows a specific circuit diagram with a marked test point and observed (faulty) result, which the student must analyze to determine the most probable fault -- not transcribed in detail here since it is a student exercise rather than a general concept.

chunks.summary: A magnitude comparator is a combinational circuit that compares two binary quantities and produces outputs indicating whether one is greater than, equal to, or less than the other.
chunks.text: A magnitude comparator is a combinational logic circuit that compares two input binary quantities and generates outputs indicating which one has the greater magnitude (or whether they are equal). As a megafunction (a larger, reusable functional building block), a magnitude comparator does not need special cascading inputs the way small comparator ICs do -- to compare wider numbers you simply specify larger data input ports on the megafunction rather than chaining multiple smaller comparator chips together.
chunks.figure_note: Page 45 shows the megafunction symbol for a magnitude comparator: two multi-bit data input ports (A and B) and three outputs (A>B, A=B, A<B).

chunks.topic: Example: Magnitude Comparator in a Digital Thermostat
chunks.summary: A digital thermostat uses two 74HC85 8-bit magnitude comparators (cascaded) to compare a digitized temperature-sensor reading against a keypad-entered setpoint, driving a furnace controller through SET/CLR logic built from cross-coupled NOR gates.
chunks.text: In a digital thermostat application, an analog temperature sensor's output is amplified and converted to an 8-bit digital value (A0-A7) by an analog-to-digital converter. A keypad encoder and register produce an 8-bit setpoint value (B0-B7) from the user's keypad entries. Two cascaded 74HC85 magnitude comparators (labeled 74HC85s) compare A against B and produce three outputs: O(A>B), O(A=B), and O(A<B). The O(A>B) output feeds a CLR (clear) path and the O(A<B) output feeds a SET path, each going through a cross-coupled pair of NOR gates that forms a simple SET/CLR latch; the latch's output drives the furnace controller, turning the furnace on when the measured temperature drops below the setpoint (A<B) and off when it rises above the setpoint (A>B).
chunks.figure_note: Page 47 (image page) shows the full thermostat block diagram: temperature sensor -> amplifier -> ADC -> A0..A7 into cascaded 74HC85 comparators (labeled 'as in Fig 9-37'); keypad -> keypad encoder/registers -> B0..B7 into the same comparators; comparator outputs O(A>B) drives CLR and O(A<B) drives SET, each routed through cross-coupled NOR gates (drawn crossed over) whose combined output drives the furnace controller block. O(A=B) is shown but not used further in this application.

chunks.summary: A code converter changes data from one binary code to another; a two-digit BCD-to-binary converter exploits the fact that each BCD bit has a fixed decimal weight (8,4,2,1 per digit, scaled by powers of 10 between digit groups) which can be converted to its binary-weighted equivalent and summed with an adder.
chunks.text: A code converter is a logic circuit that changes data presented in one type of binary code into another type of binary code. A two-digit BCD-to-binary converter is a representative example: the bits within each BCD digit group carry decimal weights of 8, 4, 2, and 1, and these weights differ by a factor of 10 from one BCD digit group (decimal digit position) to the next -- e.g. the tens-digit group's bits are effectively weighted 80, 40, 20, 10 relative to the units digit. Each BCD bit's decimal weight can be re-expressed as its equivalent binary value, and one practical way to implement the conversion logic is to sum these binary-weighted equivalents using standard binary adder circuits, producing a single pure-binary result equal to the original two-digit BCD number.

chunks.summary: A data bus is a common set of connecting lines over which multiple devices transfer data in a computer system; devices sharing a bus normally use tri-state outputs (or tri-state buffers) so that only one device drives the bus at a time, avoiding bus contention.
chunks.text: In computers, data transfer takes place over a common set of connecting lines called a data bus. Devices tied to a data bus will often have tri-state outputs, or be connected to the bus through tri-state buffers, so that a device can electrically disconnect itself from the bus (high-impedance state) when it is not the one transmitting. Devices commonly connected to a data bus include microprocessors, semiconductor memory chips, and digital-to-analog / analog-to-digital converters. In a typical example, three different devices can each transmit eight-bit data over a shared eight-line data bus to a microprocessor; only one device is enabled to drive the bus at any given time, which is essential to avoid bus contention (two devices driving conflicting logic levels onto the same line simultaneously).
chunks.figure_note: Page 52 shows a block diagram of three devices, each with tri-state 8-bit outputs, connected to a shared 8-line data bus feeding a microprocessor, with enable control ensuring only one device drives the bus at a time.

chunks.summary: The 74ALS173/HC173 is a 4-bit tri-state register: devices on a data bus contain registers (built from D flip-flops) whose outputs pass through tri-state buffers so they can be selectively connected to a shared bus, controlled by input-enable and output-enable inputs plus a common clock and master reset.
chunks.text: Devices connected to a data bus contain registers (usually built from D flip-flops) that hold the device's data. The outputs of these registers are usually connected to tri-state buffers, allowing them to be selectively tied to a shared data bus. The 74ALS173/HC173 is a specific 4-bit tri-state register IC: it has four D-type flip-flops (D0-D3 in, Q outputs), a 2-input active-LOW Input Enable (IE1-bar, IE2-bar) gate controlling whether new data D0-D3 is loaded on the clock edge, a common clock input CP, a Master Reset (MR) that asynchronously clears all four flip-flops, and a 2-input active-LOW Output Enable (OE1-bar, OE2-bar) gate controlling tri-state buffers on the four outputs O0-O3. Only when both output-enable inputs are asserted do the register's stored bits appear (in normal logic levels) on O0-O3; otherwise the outputs float to high-impedance, allowing the register to share a bus with other devices.
chunks.figure_note: Page 54 (image page) shows the full internal logic of the 74ALS173: Input Enable AND gate (IE1-bar, IE2-bar) gating D0-D3 through AND/OR combinational logic into four D flip-flops (each with CP and CLR inputs, Q/Q-bar outputs), a shared inverted clock (CP) and inverted master reset (MR) line feeding all four flip-flops, and an Output Enable AND gate (OE1-bar, OE2-bar) gating four tri-state buffers that drive outputs O0-O3 from each flip-flop's Q.

chunks.topic: Data Bus Operation: Register-to-Register Transfer and Bidirectional Lines
chunks.summary: Tri-state registers connected to a shared data bus can transfer data from any one register to another by properly sequencing their input-enable and output-enable control lines; some ICs further reduce pin count by making each bus line bidirectional (able to act as input or output depending on enable state).
chunks.text: Tristate registers connected to a data bus allow the contents of any one of several registers to be parallel-transferred over the shared bus to any other register, simply through proper application of logic levels to the registers' enable inputs: the source register's output-enable is asserted (driving its data onto the bus) while the destination register's input-enable is asserted (so it clocks in the bus data), and all other registers' output-enables stay deasserted (tri-stated) to avoid bus contention. A timing diagram illustrates the various signals involved in transferring the data value 1011 from register A to register C over the bus. A simplified way to represent this activity is a 'bus arrangement' diagram, which shows signal activity on the data bus lines schematically rather than drawing every individual connection. To further reduce the number of IC pins and bus connections, manufacturers have developed ICs where each I/O line functions as either an input or an output depending on the state of its enable inputs -- these are called bidirectional data lines, and they let a single physical pin/line serve as both a bus input and a bus output at different times.
